newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher on hopes of friendly ECI.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher on hopes of friendly ECI.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended significantly higher on Monday in a rally sparked by low Treasury financing needs and hopes for a bond-friendly labor compensation report on Tuesday.
The 30-year bond late Monday was at a session high of 102-28/32, up 21/32 from Friday. Its yield fell to 6.41 percent from 6.46 percent.
The rally came in very light volume, which, according to GovPX, was just $40 billion at 1500 EDT/1900 GMT -- when the futures market closed.
What little action there was centered on accounts setting up long positions ahead of the second-quarter Employment Cost Index due on Tuesday, traders said.

"People are not afraid to take a bullish view into the ECI," said David Connors, head trader at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "The market seems to be very confident. But there won't be a lot of follow-through even with a good number with all the long positions."
The ECI is expected to show a gain of 0.8 percent in the second quarter, after a surprisingly low 0.6 percent rise in the first quarter, according to a Reuters poll.
Last week, fears of a strong ECI increase of 1.0 percent or more weighed on Treasuries. But improved technicals have since given the market what players described as a fearless attitude.
"It is like the market is saying, 'bring it (ECI) on and we will conquer it,'" said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Securities Inc.
But Flanagan said the market could be in for a shock, particularly at the long end, if the ECI comes in strong.
"It will be difficult to rally further if we see an escalation in compensation," he said.
As was in recent weeks, the long end spearheaded the rally on Monday.
"It wasn't dramatic though, because people established the positions they wanted going to the number tomorrow," Connors said.
Treasuries had opened with a firmer tone, helped by foreign buying on the heels of a dollar that strengthened to 117.90 yen and 1.8490 marks, the highest since November 1989.
Prices edged higher throughout the day and jumped to session highs late in the afternoon after the Treasury came in with low third-quarter borrowing needs of just $10 billion.
Analysts had projected a borrowing need of at least $20 billion.
At the same time the Treasury said that it would not eliminate November's 30-year bond auction -- something that many market participants had speculated about.

In late trading, the 10-year note was up 10/32 at 103-17/32 to yield 6.14 percent. The five-year note was at 99-27/32, up 6.04 percent, to yield yielding 6.04 percent, and the two-year note was up 2/32 at 100-2/32 to yield 5.84 percent.
Three-month bills were unchanged at 5.10 percent. Six-month bills were down one basis point at 5.14 percent and year bills were down two basis points at 5.21 percent.
Also, the Treasury sold $17.0 billion three-and six-month bills at average discount rates of 5.12 percent and 5.15 percent, respectively.
